entry.title: Social Robot Navigation PhD Labs: How 20 Labs Want You to Apply

link.title: Social Robot Navigation PhD Labs: How 20 Labs Want You to Apply

entry.content:
This post covers how 20 labs that work on social robot navigation want PhD applicants to apply: which department to apply through, whether to email, what each lab looks for, and the funding and timing rules that apply. Everything comes from the labs’ own pages for prospective students.

Social robot navigation means moving a robot through spaces it shares with people, and it is my research interest and the topic of my post on simulators. When I put together a list of labs working in or near this area, the hardest part was not finding them but finding out how each one wants to be approached. Some ask you never to email. Others want an email before you apply, a form, or a PDF with a set subject line.

This post is a companion to my general guide, How to Apply to Robotics PhD Programs, which covers statements, letters, and the timeline.

Recruiting plans and pages change every year, and faculty move. Read each lab’s page yourself before you apply or write to anyone. If something here is out of date, email me and I’ll update it.

At a glance

Several of these professors don’t have a page for prospective students. For those, the usual route is to apply through the department and name them in your application.

Professor School What their page asks
Katie Driggs-Campbell UIUC Apply through ECE or CS and list Driggs-Campbell. Emails about openings are welcome but likely won’t get a reply
Joydeep Biswas UT Austin Apply through the CS PhD and name Biswas
Christoforos Mavrogiannis Michigan No prospective-student page found
Xuesu Xiao George Mason Apply, and email one PDF of materials with the subject line “[PhD Application] YOUR AFFILIATION - YOUR NAME”
Jean Oh Carnegie Mellon No prospective-student page found
Marynel Vázquez Yale Apply through Yale CS and name Vázquez
Aniket Bera Purdue Email a statement of interest, CV, transcripts, and GitHub or Scholar links
Javier Alonso-Mora TU Delft Watch for advertised vacancies, or email a CV and motivation letter
Michael Everett Northeastern Fill in the lab’s interest form, apply through ECE or Khoury, and name Everett
Jiachen Li Georgia Tech Fill in the lab’s form, and name Li in both the application and the statement. Recruiting for Spring and Fall 2027
Peter Stone UT Austin No prospective-student page found
Justin Hart UT Austin Apply through the CS PhD and list Hart. No evaluations by email
Roberto Martín-Martín UT Austin Apply through the university, use the lab’s form, and don’t send applications by email
Aaron Steinfeld Carnegie Mellon No prospective-student page found
Andrea Bajcsy Carnegie Mellon Apply through the Robotics Institute, then email with “Prospective PhD Student” in the subject line
Changliu Liu Carnegie Mellon Fill in the lab’s form
Dinesh Manocha Maryland No prospective-student page found
Rachid Alami LAAS-CNRS No prospective-student page found
Takayuki Kanda Kyoto University Contact the lab before applying to the doctoral course. Entrance exams are in August and February
Harold Soh National University of Singapore Apply to the NUS School of Computing first. The lab typically works only with NUS or exchange students

Which department

Social navigation sits between robotics, CS, and engineering, so the department you apply to depends on the lab:

  • ECE or CS. Driggs-Campbell at UIUC takes students through either ECE or CS. Everett at Northeastern takes students through ECE or the Khoury College of Computer Sciences.
  • CS only. At UT Austin, Biswas and Hart both take students through the CS PhD. Vázquez at Yale takes students through Yale’s CS PhD.
  • A robotics program. Bajcsy takes students through CMU’s Robotics Institute. Li takes students through Georgia Tech’s Robotics or Machine Learning PhD.

Apply to the program that each of your potential advisors can admit through, and name them in the application.

How to get in touch

The labs on this list cover almost every approach:

  • Don’t email; apply. Hart does not evaluate candidates by email or give feedback outside the formal admissions process. Biswas notes that a committee makes admission decisions, so Biswas can’t tell you your chances. Soh’s lab at NUS says the same: the department’s committee decides, so apply there first.
  • You can email, but don’t expect a reply. Driggs-Campbell invites prospective students to email about openings, but says a reply is unlikely because of the volume. Martín-Martín’s page also warns that emails may go unanswered, and asks applicants not to send applications directly.
  • Fill in a form. Everett’s lab says its interest form is not an application, but it lets the lab look at your background when emails can’t all be answered. The lab takes multiple students each cycle. Li’s, Martín-Martín’s, and Liu’s labs also use forms. You still apply through the university.
  • Email after you apply. Bajcsy is less likely to reply to emails sent before the mid-December deadline. After you apply through the Robotics Institute, email with “Prospective PhD Student” in the subject line, your CV, your research interests, and why you want to join the lab.
  • Email your materials with your application. Xiao asks PhD applicants to apply to George Mason and also email a single PDF with a cover letter, CV, transcript, three references, and relevant publications, with the subject line “[PhD Application] YOUR AFFILIATION - YOUR NAME”. Bera asks for an email with a short statement of interest, a CV, transcripts, and links to your GitHub or Google Scholar.
  • Email first. Kanda’s lab at Kyoto asks doctoral applicants to get in touch before applying, to discuss their research background and interests. Alonso-Mora’s group at TU Delft posts PhD positions as vacancies, and also welcomes unsolicited applications sent with a CV and a motivation letter.

The labs that want contact first are outside the US, in Japan and the Netherlands. Singapore is the exception: Soh’s lab defers to the department and typically can’t work with students who aren’t at NUS or on an official exchange.

What they look for

These labs agree that you need research experience, but they weigh real robots, learning, and publications differently:

  • Real robots. Biswas looks for self-motivated students with a strong mathematical background who pick up new tools quickly. Any major is fine; Biswas’s students have come from math, physics, EE, ME, and CS. The lab focuses on “solving problems, not promoting tools,” and deploys its work on physical robots rather than only in simulation. Martín-Martín looks for people eager to create new methods in robot learning, perception, control, and planning, and says it helps if you enjoy working with real robots in the real world.
  • Hardware and field work. Xiao strongly prefers applicants with hands-on robotics hardware experience, field experience, and a good publication record.
  • Publications. Hart looks for strong academic preparation, prior research experience, and publications at major robotics venues such as ICRA, IROS, HRI, and RO-MAN.
  • Perception and learning. Bera’s IDEAS Lab wants a strong background in computer vision and machine learning, especially human detection, tracking, and motion prediction, plus deep learning frameworks, experience collecting and annotating data, interest in real-time and edge hardware, and the motivation to publish.
  • Coding and communication. Li’s TASL lab requires strong analytical and coding skills and good written and spoken English, and prefers Python or C++, PyTorch or TensorFlow, robot programming, and prior research.

Publications are where these labs differ most from the general advice. The CMU guide that many professors recommend says you don’t need a publication to be admitted. Hart and Xiao, on the other hand, list them among what they look for.

If you are a master’s student

Two of these labs give master’s students a concrete way in:

  • Xiao’s RobotiXX lab says one way to stand out is to set up the simulation environments of The BARN Challenge, a navigation competition, and build a method that performs well, preferably better than the baselines. Master’s students in the lab first join projects led by senior students, with the hope of continuing to a doctorate, and assistantships can open up after one or two semesters of strong research.
  • Bera’s lab says exceptional BS and MS students may be considered for the PhD program based on their performance and research fit.

Funding and timing

  • Bajcsy’s page says students who are applying for or already hold an external fellowship are of particular interest, because self-funded students make it easier to find a spot in the lab.
  • Kanda’s lab hosts only MEXT scholars recommended by the Japanese embassy in their home country. International applicants apply through the embassy first and contact the lab after passing its screening. Kyoto holds entrance exams in August for April enrollment and in February for October enrollment.
  • Li is recruiting several fully funded PhD students for Spring 2027 as well as Fall 2027, so not every lab follows the fall-only calendar.
  • Faculty move. Li, for example, was at UC Riverside and is now at Georgia Tech. Check where each professor is now before you build your list.

Links

  • Katie Driggs-Campbell, homepage and Human-Centered Autonomy Lab, UIUC
  • Joydeep Biswas, Prospective Students, UT Austin
  • Christoforos Mavrogiannis, homepage and lab, University of Michigan
  • Xuesu Xiao, RobotiXX Opportunities, George Mason University
  • Jean Oh, Bot Intelligence Group, Carnegie Mellon
  • Marynel Vázquez, Open Positions, Yale
  • Aniket Bera, Research Opportunity with the IDEAS Lab, Purdue
  • Javier Alonso-Mora, Vacancies, TU Delft
  • Michael Everett, Join Us, Northeastern
  • Jiachen Li, Join TASL, Georgia Tech
  • Peter Stone, homepage, UT Austin
  • Justin Hart, How to Join My Lab, UT Austin
  • Roberto Martín-Martín, Apply to RobIN, UT Austin
  • Aaron Steinfeld, homepage, Carnegie Mellon
  • Andrea Bajcsy, Join the Lab, Carnegie Mellon
  • Changliu Liu, Intelligent Control Lab, Carnegie Mellon
  • Dinesh Manocha, GAMMA, University of Maryland
  • Rachid Alami, homepage, LAAS-CNRS
  • Takayuki Kanda, Join Us, Kyoto University
  • Harold Soh, About CLeAR, National University of Singapore

entry.title: How to Apply to Robotics PhD Programs: A Practical Guide

link.title: How to Apply to Robotics PhD Programs: A Practical Guide

entry.content:
This guide covers how to apply to a robotics PhD program: when to start research, which program to apply to, how to approach professors, what goes in a statement of purpose, how to get strong letters, and the timeline. It draws on my own applications and on what professors and robotics programs have written about how they admit students.

Robotics PhD students are admitted through robotics programs and through CS, ECE, and mechanical engineering departments, so much of the general CS advice applies. The main general source is Mor Harchol-Balter’s Applying to Ph.D. Programs in Computer Science (CMU), written by someone who has served on PhD admissions at CMU, Berkeley, and MIT. Robotics professors still point applicants to it, including Joydeep Biswas at UT Austin. The robotics-specific advice comes from program pages and from robotics professors’ pages for prospective students. Where sources disagree, I describe each view. All of them are listed in Links at the end.

The CMU guide was last updated in 2014, so its numbers on stipends, the GRE, and rankings are dated. Its advice on research, letters, and statements still holds. Professors’ recruiting plans change every year, so check their pages yourself. If something here is out of date, email me and I’ll update it.

Start research early

You apply to a PhD about a year before you start it. Applications are usually due in December or January, and the program begins the following fall. By the time you apply, you need research experience, professors who can write about it, and some confidence that you want to spend five or six more years doing research.

That last part is easy to underestimate. The CMU guide says: “Do not even think of applying for a Ph.D. if you have not tried research and/or teaching and found that you like at least one of those.” Knowing that you enjoy going deep into one problem usually comes only after you have done research for a while. Because applications go out a year ahead, you need to know this a year early.

For many master’s students, the timing doesn’t work out. I did my MS at UC Riverside, which runs on ten-week quarters. As an international student, my priority was to finish quickly, mostly for financial reasons, and I completed the degree in one year and three months, including a three-month summer break. In a program that short, PhD deadlines arrive while you are still taking classes. The final months often go to chasing a first publication, working day and night on a project, and applying to jobs as a backup. The realization that you want to do research may come near the end of the degree, when the deadlines are close or already past.

My advice is to start research in your first term, even in a small way. A few months of real research before your final term gives you something to write about, a professor who can write your letter, and time to find out whether you want a PhD at all.

To find a research position at your own school, the CMU guide suggests going to a professor’s office hours or emailing for a meeting, bringing a one-page summary of your background and interests, and expecting to ask several professors before one says yes. In robotics, hands-on work also counts. Duke Robotics points master’s students who want research toward an independent study with a faculty member, which can grow into a thesis, and toward its robotics club, which competes in RoboSub.

Some labs suggest specific projects. For navigation, Xuesu Xiao’s RobotiXX lab at George Mason says one way to stand out is to set up the simulation environments of The BARN Challenge, a navigation competition, and build a method that performs well, preferably better than the baselines. A result like that is something you can finish during a short master’s, and it gives you a concrete project to write about.

If you reach the deadlines without enough research, waiting a year is a real option. Tim Dettmers writes about extending a master’s by a year to do research internships, and credits those internships for the PhD admissions that followed. The CMU guide suggests working in a research lab for a few years if you are unsure. Sonia Roberts on Robohub argues that a few years in industry can build savings, show you whether you really want a PhD, and make you a stronger applicant.

Some labs also offer a path from a master’s into the PhD. At RobotiXX, master’s students first join projects led by senior students, with the hope of continuing to a doctorate, and assistantships can open up after one or two semesters of strong research. Aniket Bera’s IDEAS Lab at Purdue says exceptional BS and MS students may be considered for the PhD program based on their performance and research fit.

What a PhD involves

The CMU guide describes a PhD as “a long, in depth research exploration of one topic.” That means about six years, few courses, and by the end, one narrow problem you know better than anyone. Research differs from classes in a few ways. Problems don’t come with known answers, and finding a good problem is part of the job. There are no grades, so you have to motivate yourself. You meet your advisor for about an hour a week, so you have to plan how to use that time.

The guide’s list of what a PhD takes deliberately leaves out being smart. Perseverance and a clear reason for wanting the degree matter more.

The Robohub article compares a robotics PhD with going straight into industry, which is worth reading if you are applying to both:

  • A PhD works more like a job than more school. You set your own research questions, while industry roles usually come with smaller, well-defined goals and a team.
  • Academic research can have a large impact, but rarely an immediate one. The article names frustration with slow, invisible impact as a major source of burnout.
  • The pay gap is large. Its example compares a $100,000 entry-level job with a $40,000 stipend over six years, which comes to roughly $400,000 in lost earnings once raises are included.
  • A PhD is required for some jobs, mostly in academia. In industry it is often treated as roughly equal to a few years of work experience.

The article’s conclusion is that a PhD makes sense if you enjoy open-ended, self-directed research or want the specific jobs it leads to, not for prestige.

Which program to apply to

Robotics faculty sit in different departments, and the way you apply depends on the school:

  • A robotics PhD through a home school. At Georgia Tech, you apply to the Robotics PhD through one of five home schools: Interactive Computing, Aerospace, Biomedical, Electrical and Computer, or Mechanical Engineering. Your home school also sets some requirements, such as a teaching practicum. In the College of Computing, the GRE is optional for the Robotics PhD.
  • A department, chosen with your advisor. Duke Robotics advises PhD applicants to contact the faculty member they want to work with before applying. If that professor is taking students and sees a fit, they will say which department to apply to: mechanical engineering, ECE, or CS.
  • Any of several departments, as long as you name the professor. Michael Posa’s DAIR Lab at Penn takes students through mechanical engineering (MEAM), ESE, or CIS, and asks you to name Posa in your application. Erdem Bıyık at USC reviews applications the same way in CS and ECE, and advises choosing based on the other faculty you would want to work with. Katie Driggs-Campbell at UIUC takes students through ECE or CS.
  • One department. Tom Silver’s lab at Princeton takes students through ECE. Francesco Bullo at UCSB asks applicants to apply to mechanical engineering or a related department. At UT Austin, Biswas takes students through the CS PhD.

Before applying, find out which programs each of your potential advisors can admit through. Then pick the one whose courses and qualifying exams suit you best.

What robotics labs look for

“Robotics” covers very different work, and labs ask for different backgrounds. Compare four pages:

  • Junaed Sattar’s lab at Minnesota tests its research on physical robots, often outdoors, so it wants strong coding skills and an interest in robots themselves. Hardware experience with microcontrollers, sensors, and actuators is a plus. Applicants mainly interested in computer vision, deep learning, or language, without a strong interest in robotics, are unlikely to fit.
  • Seyed Amir Tafrishi at Cardiff warns that robotics involves heavy mathematics, drawing on control theory, mechanics, electronics, and materials, not just AI. Applicants without an engineering background or robotics and controls coursework are unlikely to be considered.
  • Bullo values strong mathematical preparation over the specific undergraduate major.
  • AJung Moon at McGill, who works on robot ethics and human-robot interaction, welcomes backgrounds in policy, ethics, and psychology as well as engineering. Moon lists teamwork and curiosity among the main qualities sought, and says grades are not the first or only thing considered.

Labs within a single subfield differ in the same way. In social robot navigation, Biswas looks for a strong mathematical background from any major, with a focus on “solving problems, not promoting tools,” and deploys the lab’s work on physical robots. Bera’s IDEAS Lab instead asks for computer vision and machine learning, especially detecting, tracking, and predicting the motion of people. I compared 20 social navigation labs in a separate post, Social Navigation PhD Labs.

So “robotics” alone doesn’t describe what you want to do. Tafrishi asks applicants not to write vague statements like “AI” or “robotics.” Name the problem, such as navigation in crowds, manipulation, or legged locomotion, and the methods you have used.

Two programs publish how their faculty judge applications. Oregon State Robotics lists five criteria: academic preparation, research experience, extracurricular activities that show drive and collaboration, work that makes robotics and STEM more inclusive (outreach, tutoring, mentoring), and alignment with the program, for which you name 2–3 faculty you would like as advisors. At Michigan Robotics, twelve faculty each answered the question in their own words, and they don’t all agree:

  • Publications. Yulun Tian looks for publications or substantial projects, and Mark Draelos for sustained academic excellence in courses, projects, or publications. Jessy Grizzle, by contrast, looks at applicants from smaller schools for class projects they pushed beyond what was required.
  • GPA. Grizzle says a perfect GPA isn’t necessary, and Yanran Ding values technical depth and a clear story over a perfect GPA. Anouck Girard asks for evidence of excellent scholarship.
  • Personality versus technical depth. Brent Gillespie wants to hear a distinct personality in the essays. Talia Moore wants to know what gaps you see in the field and how you would address them.
  • Independence. Lionel Robert looks for the shift from a strong student to an independent scholar who can frame problems and handle negative feedback.

What they share is a preference for specific, detailed descriptions of your own projects: your role, what went wrong, and what you learned. Patricia Alves-Oliveira asks applicants to go beyond buzzwords.

Contacting professors

Professors disagree most about whether you should email them before applying. Read each professor’s page before you write to anyone. The sources here range from “please don’t” to “please do”:

  • Don’t email; apply through the portal. Bıyık stopped answering PhD inquiry emails after receiving 50–100 a month, and reviews every application that lists Bıyık as a potential advisor. Sattar considers only applications submitted through the university’s admissions system, and ignores emails about research unrelated to the lab. Posa writes that the lab can’t respond to all unsolicited emails. Justin Hart at UT Austin does not evaluate candidates by email or give feedback outside the formal admissions process.
  • You can email, but don’t expect a reply. Driggs-Campbell invites prospective students to email about openings, but says a reply is unlikely because of the volume, and encourages applying through ECE or CS and listing Driggs-Campbell as a faculty member of interest.
  • No need to email, but you can. Silver’s lab page says there is no need to email ahead of time, although you are welcome to. Marynel Vázquez at Yale asks PhD applicants to apply and name Vázquez in the application.
  • Fill in the lab’s form. A growing number of labs use an interest form instead of email. Michael Everett’s lab at Northeastern says the form is not an application, but it lets the lab look at your background when emails can’t all be answered. You still apply through the university.
  • Email after you apply. Bullo asks you to study the group’s papers first, apply, and then send one email saying you have applied. Bullo asks people not to email repeatedly and is unlikely to offer funding before knowing a student well or getting a strong recommendation from someone Bullo knows. Andrea Bajcsy’s lab at CMU is less likely to reply to emails sent before the deadline, and asks for one after you have applied, with “Prospective PhD Student” in the subject line.
  • Email your materials along with your application. Xiao asks PhD applicants to apply to George Mason and also email a single PDF with a cover letter, CV, transcript, references, and publications, under a set subject line.
  • Email first. Duke Robotics strongly advises contacting advisors in advance. At Michigan, Steven Ceron asks applicants to email a CV. Moon’s process at McGill starts with an email, with a set subject line: “(Domestic/International) Prospective Student for (start date) (PhD/M.Sc.) – (Your Name)”. In it, Moon asks you to name a paper of the lab’s that interested you and ask a question it raised, describe your research experience, and attach a CV and a writing sample. Tafrishi, at a UK university, asks for a CV, transcripts, up to 2–3 papers, and a short research proposal, and also gives a subject-line format. Takayuki Kanda’s HRI lab at Kyoto University asks doctoral applicants to get in touch before applying, to discuss their research background and interests.

In these examples, the professors who ask for an email first are mostly outside the US, in Canada, the UK, and Japan, or in departments where the advisor picks students directly. Not every country outside the US works this way: Harold Soh’s lab at NUS in Singapore defers to the department’s admissions committee. Dettmers notes the same broad pattern: emailing first is not required in the US but sometimes is in Europe. Dettmers also says that cold emails without a personal connection rarely get read, and that contact works best when one of your letter writers introduces you.

Before reaching out, check:

  1. Is there a “prospective students” page or FAQ? Read all of it.
  2. Are they recruiting for your cycle, and for which start term? Moon, for example, is not taking students for Fall 2026 or Winter 2027, and Bullo is unlikely to have a position for 2027/28. Jiachen Li’s lab at Georgia Tech, on the other hand, is looking for several fully funded PhD students starting in Spring or Fall 2027.
  3. Which departments can they admit students through?
  4. Do they want an email, a mention in your statement, or just your application through the portal? If they give a subject-line format, use it exactly.

If you do email, be specific. A CV and GPA alone don’t say why you fit. Moon notes that a high GPA doesn’t show research or teamwork, and Sattar notes that a CV and publication list may not be enough to judge fit.

Example: social navigation labs

My own research interest is social robot navigation, the topic of my post on simulators. Among the 20 labs I looked at in that area, every approach above shows up: Hart asks for no email, Driggs-Campbell welcomes one but probably won’t reply, Everett uses a form, Bajcsy wants an email only after you apply, Xiao wants a PDF with a set subject line, and Kanda wants contact first. Seven of the 20 have no page for prospective students at all. The full comparison, with what each lab looks for, is in Social Navigation PhD Labs.

Choosing where to apply

Most of this comes from the CMU guide’s section on choosing a program:

  • Count the faculty in your area, leaving out anyone listed on the website who has moved elsewhere. Do the same for two other areas you might enjoy, since about half of students change their research area.
  • Count the faculty whose work excites you and who are taking students. That is your real pool of possible advisors. Dettmers gives the same advice: choose universities mainly by possible advisors, and prefer programs with more than one.
  • Talk to current students, and former ones too. Ask how often they meet their advisor and whether they are excited about their work. Chaitanya Joshi points out that a professor who seems friendly on social media may run a very different lab, and that you are picking the advisor as much as they are picking you. At Michigan, Ram Vasudevan also encourages applicants to contact the lab’s current and former students.
  • Ask how funding works. At some schools you can only work with advisors who have grants, and if your advisor loses funding you may end up as a teaching assistant every term.
  • Rankings matter mostly for your peers, who are the people you will learn the most from. A famous professor is not necessarily a good advisor.
  • Consider cost of living. The same stipend goes much further in some cities, and the difference adds up over six years.

On how many schools to apply to, the sources differ. The CMU guide suggests about three schools at your level, two above it, and one or two below it, around six or seven in total. Dettmers suggests 10–15, including one or two where admission is very likely, and warns that more than that leaves too little time to polish each application. Application fees and the time each statement takes are the real limits.

Include schools that are strong in your specific area even if they rank lower overall. To judge your level for a particular lab, look at its current PhD students and what they had done when they applied.

What committees look for

For top programs, research experience matters most, along with what your letters and statement say about it. How much a publication matters is where sources differ:

  • The CMU guide says you don’t need a publication or a finished result. The committee needs to see that you know what doing research is like. Applicants with a 4.0 GPA and no research are considered high risk and are usually rejected.
  • Dettmers ranks recommendation letters above publications.
  • Bullo lists publications in international venues, a degree from a top school, and letters from internationally known professors among the things that help. Hart looks for publications at ICRA, IROS, HRI, or RO-MAN, and Xiao strongly prefers a good publication record.
  • At Michigan, as above, some faculty look for publications and others accept strong class projects, especially from smaller schools.

On grades, most sources agree that past a certain point they stop mattering. The CMU guide says around 3.5/4.0 in CS, math, and engineering is fine, judged relative to your school, and that time on research is worth more than raising a 3.5 to a 4.0. Dettmers says anything above 3.5 doesn’t matter and treats the GRE as a filter. Many programs, including Georgia Tech’s Robotics PhD, no longer require the GRE.

International applicants should publish in venues the committee will recognize and put English versions of their papers on a personal website.

Research experience can come from a professor at your school, a summer program such as an REU, a research job in industry, an MS project or thesis, robotics competitions, or reading recent conference papers on your own and trying to improve on one.

Statement of purpose

Despite the name, the statement of purpose is a research statement. The committee wants to know what research you have done, what you want to do next, and why you like research. The CMU guide suggests this structure:

  1. Paragraph 1: The research areas that interest you, and why. This helps route your application to the right faculty.
  2. Paragraphs 2–4: The projects you worked on. What was the problem, why did it matter, what did you try, and what did you learn? It is fine to say you didn’t fully solve it.
  3. Paragraph 5: Why you need a PhD in particular.
  4. Paragraph 6: Why this school. Name the faculty you would like to work with and papers of theirs you have read.

The Stanford CS advice, collected from current PhD students, describes a similar shape: an introduction that names your area and summarizes your research experience in one sentence, body paragraphs that each tell one focused story about a project, and a final paragraph that is specific to the school. Only that last paragraph usually changes between schools. Its other tips:

  • Statements are commonly about two pages. They run long when they go too deep into technical details or repeat the whole CV.
  • For each project, explain why the problem was worth solving, what you personally contributed, what you learned, and what didn’t work off the shelf and why.
  • Use the active voice (“I built,” “we published”), and consider short bold headers to label each project.

Some programs ask for two essays. Michigan Robotics wants an academic statement (about a page that goes deep on your past research, then half a page on future interests and the faculty whose work fits them) and a separate personal statement about your path and motivation. It asks you not to summarize a paper’s abstract, and to split any overlapping topic so the two essays don’t repeat each other.

Naming faculty is expected almost everywhere. Oregon State asks for 2–3 names, and Bullo, Posa, Silver, and Vázquez all ask to be named. At Michigan, Grizzle says naming faculty is not essential. Naming an area is not a commitment either: about a third of students end up working on something else.

How to open

Andy Pavlo (CMU) wrote a short post on how to write a bad statement, built from openings read on the admissions committee. The most common is the boy genius: a story about how early you fell in love with computers. Pavlo sorts real examples by age, from “When I was 6, my father bought a computer for me” through middle school and high school. Pavlo credits Harchol-Balter with the earliest one: “When I was born, my mother gave me a glass ball to play with.” The CMU guide’s verdict on these is blunt: “We simply don’t care what you did as a child, and we don’t believe you either.” The Stanford advice gives a similar example to avoid: “Ever since I was a child, I have been interested in unraveling the mysteries of intelligence…”

The college version is the class epiphany: a course you took made you want a PhD. Pavlo’s point is that this shows what you sat through, not what you did. The CMU guide adds one more mistake: repeating grades and test scores that the committee can already see elsewhere in the application.

The sources differ on how much style the opening needs. Pavlo would rather read a plain statement of your research interests, even a dry one, than an irrelevant story. Dettmers calls the first paragraph the most important part and recommends a hook that makes the reader want to continue. Both start with your research interests. If you use a hook, make it about something you built or a problem you worked on, such as a research project, a paper, an open-source tool, or a robot.

Write it yourself

At Michigan, Gillespie writes that essays which seem AI-generated are an immediate turn-off, and several faculty there ask for a genuine voice. Faculty read hundreds of statements, and generic phrasing stands out. Use tools to check grammar if you like, but the ideas and the voice should be yours.

Get feedback

Ask your professors, labmates, and other applicants to read drafts, as Joshi recommends. Some schools have students who review applications before they are submitted. At CMU, the student-run Robotics Institute Graduate Application Support Program matches PhD and MSR applicants with a current RI student who gives feedback on their materials. Spots go first-come, first-served, so sign up early.

Your CV

The Stanford advice also covers the CV. Keep it to one or two pages, with education, research experience, and publications on the first page. A short publications list is fine, and papers under review can be listed if they are clearly labeled. Start each bullet with a strong verb, and keep bullets to about one line. Tafrishi suggests including robotics competitions, conference attendance, documented robot projects, and robotics or controls courses.

Recommendation letters

The CMU guide calls letters “perhaps the most important part of your application,” and Dettmers agrees, ranking them above publications. Most programs ask for three.

A letter that only says you got an A and never missed class adds nothing, because your transcript already shows that. A strong letter describes you doing research and taking initiative. Words like self-motivated, independent, and strong research potential carry weight. Several Michigan faculty also look for letters that show you working both independently and in a team. Dettmers suggests choosing writers who highlight different strengths, rather than three letters that say the same thing.

Ask people who have seen you do research. Letters from professors count most, followed by research scientists, then lecturers, employers, and postdocs. Avoid letters from graduate students. If a graduate student supervised you, ask their professor to co-write the letter. A letter carries more weight when the committee knows the writer and the writer can compare you to current PhD students.

When you ask, phrase it as: “Do you feel comfortable writing a strong letter of recommendation for me to graduate school?” This gives them an easy way to decline, which is better than a weak letter. Then send each writer:

  • Your statement of purpose
  • A summary of each research project, who you worked with, and any papers or reports
  • Your math, CS, engineering, and science courses, with professors and grades
  • Awards and activities outside class
  • A due date a little earlier than the real one, and a note that you will send a reminder

Confirm with each school that every letter arrived, and thank your writers afterward. Missing letters can keep your application from being reviewed in time.

Funding and fellowships

Most US robotics and CS PhD programs cover tuition and pay a stipend through a research assistantship, funded by your advisor’s grants, or a teaching assistantship. At schools without guaranteed funding, your choice of advisor may be limited to those with grants.

Funding also affects deadlines. Sattar’s lab and Oregon State both use December 15 as the deadline for funding consideration, and later applications may be reviewed only after that pool. Moon notes that grant funding for a September start often isn’t clear until early May, so silence before then may not be a no.

Apply for outside fellowships, such as the NSF GRFP, NDSEG, and Hertz, before you have chosen schools. They fund several years, let you work with any advisor, and strengthen your application. Many require US citizenship or permanent residency, so check the current rules. Outside the US, mention scholarships you have won or applied for. Moon asks for these in the first email, and Tafrishi asks for the scholarship name in the subject line. Fellowship deadlines are usually one to two months before school deadlines.

A fellowship can also make a lab more willing to take you. Bajcsy’s page says students who are applying for or already hold an external fellowship are of particular interest, because self-funded students make it easier to find a spot in the lab. In Japan, Kanda’s lab hosts only MEXT scholars recommended by the Japanese embassy in their home country, so international applicants apply through the embassy first and contact the lab after passing its screening.

Application fees add up across many schools. Fee waivers are handled by the university, not by individual professors, so check each school’s eligibility rules.

Timeline

Exact dates vary by school, so check each one. This table follows the usual US calendar. Some labs also admit students in the spring, such as Li’s lab at Georgia Tech. Outside the US the calendar can be entirely different: Kyoto University holds entrance exams in August for April enrollment and in February for October enrollment.

When What
First term of your degree Start research. Get to know the professors who might write your letters
Summer / early fall before you apply Build your list of schools and advisors. Read each professor’s prospective-students page. Ask for letters. Sign up for review programs
1–2 months before school deadlines Submit fellowship applications
December–January Submit applications. Many funding deadlines are around December 15. Confirm every letter arrived
January–February Interviews with interested faculty
By March Decisions arrive. If you haven’t heard, email the admissions contact
March–April Visit days. Go if you can; talking to current students is the best way to judge a lab
April 15 The usual deadline to accept an offer at US schools

Links

General guides:

  • Mor Harchol-Balter, Applying to Ph.D. Programs in Computer Science, CMU, 2014
  • Andy Pavlo, How to Write a Bad Statement for a Computer Science Ph.D. Admissions Application, CMU, 2015
  • Tim Dettmers, Machine Learning PhD Applications: Everything You Need to Know, 2018. A complete walkthrough, from choosing schools to letters.
  • Chaitanya Joshi, PhD Application Advice for Machine Learning and Artificial Intelligence, 2021 (archived copy). An annotated list of other guides.
  • Stanford CS, General Advice for CS PhD Applicants. Statement and CV advice collected from current PhD students.

Robotics programs:

  • University of Michigan Robotics, What are specific faculty looking for in PhD applications?, 2024, and Academic and Personal Statements
  • Oregon State Robotics, Graduate Application Advice
  • Georgia Tech, Ph.D. Program in Robotics
  • Duke Robotics, For Prospective Graduate Students
  • CMU Robotics Institute, Graduate Application Support Program (student-run)
  • Sonia Roberts, Careers in robotics: Should you get a PhD or go into industry?, Robohub, 2022

Professors’ pages for prospective students:

  • Erdem Bıyık, Prospective Students and Postdocs, USC Lira Lab
  • Marynel Vázquez, Open Positions, Yale
  • Francesco Bullo, Advice for Prospective Students, UCSB
  • Junaed Sattar, For Prospective Students, University of Minnesota
  • AJung Moon, Prospective Students, McGill
  • Michael Posa, Joining DAIR Lab, Penn
  • Tom Silver, PRPL Lab, Princeton
  • Seyed Amir Tafrishi, Prospective Students, Cardiff University

entry.title: How to Install Arena-Rosnav and SEAN: Social Navigation Simulators

link.title: How to Install Arena-Rosnav and SEAN: Social Navigation Simulators

entry.content:
This guide covers how to install Arena-Rosnav (Arena) and SEAN, two of the most complete open-source simulators for social robot navigation: which version to pick for your ROS distro, which simulators each version actually runs, and how to fix the install errors that come up most often.

Social robot navigation means moving a robot through spaces it shares with people: keeping a comfortable distance, waiting at a doorway, going around a group instead of through it, and moving in a way people can predict. The obstacles have intentions, and they react to the robot as much as it reacts to them. Robots like the one below, which collects used dishes at a Starbucks in Singapore, already do this in cafés, and more are coming to hospitals, airports, and offices.

Testing with real crowds is slow, expensive, and sometimes unsafe, so most research starts in simulation. Arena and SEAN have each gone through several versions, and each version has its own paper, code, ROS distro, and docs, which don’t always agree. Finding the exact version a paper used can take days.

If you’re new to social navigation, start with the table below. If you’re reproducing a specific paper, go to the version tables and to When the install breaks. Every link in the post is also collected in Links at the end.

If something here is out of date, email me and I’ll update it.

Which one should I install?

Your ROS version decides most of this, so start there:

If you want… Start with
The newest Arena, with Isaac Sim or MuJoCo (ROS 2 Jazzy, Docker) Arena 5.0: voshch/Arena
ROS 2 Humble on Ubuntu 22.04, with Gazebo Arena 4.0: humble branch of Arena-Rosnav/arena-rosnav
ROS 1 Noetic on Ubuntu 20.04, with Flatland, Gazebo, or Unity Arena 3.0: master branch of Arena-Rosnav/arena-rosnav
The code from the original 2021 paper ignc-research/arena-rosnav
Unity with scripted social situations SEAN 2.0: yale-sean/social_sim_unity
A lightweight 2D sandbox for reinforcement learning CrowdNav or ir-sim

The rest of the post explains where these come from and how to install each one.

Arena

Arena comes from Linh Kästner and Volodymyr Shcherbyna, along with many collaborators. Linh now leads the ARENA Lab at Singapore Management University. Arena is a whole platform rather than just a simulator: it generates worlds, simulates pedestrians, comes with more than 30 planners (from classical to learning-based and vision-language ones), and includes pipelines for training and benchmarking. In its repos, it’s usually called Arena-Rosnav.

Eight papers in five years

Arena started in 2021 as a 2D simulator for training reinforcement learning planners. A Gazebo version followed, the 2022 Arena-Bench paper turned both into a benchmark, and with Arena-Rosnav 2.0 in 2023 the code moved to a new GitHub organization. Version 3.0 (2024) focused on social navigation on ROS 1, 4.0 (2025) moved to ROS 2, and 5.0 (2025) added NVIDIA Isaac Sim. Each step came with its own paper and its own place in the code:

Version Venue Code ROS
Arena-Rosnav IROS 2021 ignc-research/arena-rosnav (Gazebo: arena-rosnav-3D) ROS 1
Arena-Bench RA-L/IROS 2022 ignc-research/arena-bench ROS 1
Arena-Rosnav 2.0 IROS 2023 Arena-Rosnav/arena-rosnav, tags v0.1.0 to v0.2.2 ROS 1
Arena-Web RSS 2023 - -
Arena 3.0 RSS 2024 master branch of Arena-Rosnav/arena-rosnav ROS 1 Noetic
Arena 4.0 ICRA 2025 humble branch of Arena-Rosnav/arena-rosnav ROS 2 Humble
Arena 5.0 RSS 2025 humble branch at the time, now voshch/Arena ROS 2 Humble, now Jazzy
Arena-Bench 2.0 IROS 2025 Arena-Rosnav org ROS 2

Note that the papers point to the Arena-Rosnav GitHub organization, but the project pages now link voshch/Arena, Volodymyr’s own repo, which he created in October 2025. If you’re reproducing a specific paper, the branches and tags of Arena-Rosnav/arena-rosnav are closer to what it used. The group has since released PEDS, a newer benchmark accepted to RA-L in 2026.

Which simulators does each version really support?

The simulator decides what you install, and papers, project pages, and code don’t always list the same ones.

Take Arena 5.0. Figure 2 of its paper puts the Gazebo, Unity, and NVIDIA Isaac logos side by side, and the text calls Unity and Isaac its photorealistic simulators. The project page lists four: Isaac Sim, Unity, Gazebo, and Flatland. In the code, however, Unity doesn’t run on ROS 2.

Unity support only ever existed on the ROS 1 branch, as a prebuilt binary last released in June 2024. When Arena 5.0 was presented at RSS in June 2025, its code could launch Gazebo or Isaac Sim. Today’s code adds MuJoCo and flatsim, a new 2D simulator that is not the older Flatland. That matches what the main Arena site lists now, so trust the main site over the 5.0 project page.

The paper also mentions Isaac Gym, but the code uses Isaac Sim, which is a different NVIDIA product. Search for Isaac Sim when you debug.

Here is the full picture for every version:

Version The paper says The code runs
Arena-Rosnav (2021) A 2D simulator Flatland, with Gazebo in a separate repo
Arena-Bench (2022) Flatland, Gazebo Flatland, Gazebo
Arena-Rosnav 2.0 (2023) Flatland, Gazebo, Unity, Arena2D Flatland and Gazebo, with Unity and Arena2D in separate repos
Arena 3.0 (2024) Flatland, Gazebo, Unity Flatland, Gazebo Classic, Unity
Arena 4.0 (2025) Gazebo Garden, Unity Gazebo Garden at first, now Gazebo Harmonic plus optional Isaac Sim 4.2
Arena 5.0 (2025) Isaac, Gazebo, Unity Gazebo and Isaac Sim 4.2 at RSS; today Isaac Sim 6.1, Gazebo Harmonic, MuJoCo, flatsim
Arena-Bench 2.0 (2025) Gazebo, Unity, Isaac Sim Gazebo and Isaac Sim 4.2

In short: if you need Unity, use Arena 3.0 on ROS 1. If you need Isaac Sim, use 5.0.

Which docs go with which version?

Each version has its own docs site, and the older ones have moved or disappeared:

  • Arena 5.0: docs.arena-rosnav.org, generated from the voshch/Arena READMEs. The old arena-dev.readthedocs.io address redirects there.
  • Arena 4.0: arena-rosnav.readthedocs.io, which covers the humble branch.
  • Arena 3.0: no longer hosted. Its installation and usage guides survive in the arena3 tag of the Arena-Rosnav/.github repo.

Most branch READMEs still link to pages that no longer exist, so always match the docs to the branch you cloned. Two more things look current but aren’t: the Arena-Rosnav GitHub profile is titled “Arena 5.0” but links to the humble branch and the 4.0 docs, and the worksheets at edu.arena-rosnav.org were written for 3.0.

Branch-by-branch notes

These are the main branches of Arena-Rosnav/arena-rosnav:

Branch What it is
master ROS 1 (Arena 3.0). Its README’s install link returns 404, so use the arena3 guide instead. install4_arena_unity.sh adds Unity.
humble ROS 2 Humble (Arena 4.0, then the first Isaac Sim work). Its README’s install link works.
ros2 An earlier ROS 2 port, last updated in July 2024 and replaced by humble. Its install link returns 404.
unity-simulator The ROS 1 branch where Unity support was built, merged into master in February 2024. Its install link returns 404.
dev A ROS 1 development branch from April 2023, with manual catkin and Poetry steps.

The code from before 2023 lives in ignc-research/arena-rosnav, which hasn’t been maintained since early 2023. Its default branch, local_planner_subgoalmode, matches the 2021 paper, and it has around 40 thesis and experiment branches. The ivaROS lab’s fork, ivaROS/arena-rosnav, has a three-script install for Ubuntu 20.04, plus social_nav, learn_social, and social_cost_function branches.

Installing Arena

Once you know your version, installing is mostly one script. What differs is how much each script asks of your machine.

Arena 5.0: ROS 2 Jazzy in Docker

This is the easiest path if you have an NVIDIA GPU. ROS 2 runs inside a container, so your host stays clean. You need Docker (with your user in the docker group) or Podman, plus the NVIDIA Container Toolkit:

curl https://raw.githubusercontent.com/voshch/Arena/jazzy/install.sh > install.sh
bash install.sh
cd ~/arena_ws && source arena
arena feature isaac install   # or gazebo / mujoco / flatsim / training
arena launch sim:=isaac

The installer clones Arena into ~/arena_ws and sets up its container. Install at least one simulator before you launch. For reinforcement learning training, also run arena feature docker gpu on, then source arena again. If you change your mind later, source arena uninstall removes the containers and images, and adding --all deletes your data and caches too.

Two things to know before you start. First, the jazzy branch moves fast: MuJoCo and flatsim arrived in October 2026, and the only release so far is a v0.0.1 pre-release from March 2026, so write down the commit you used. Second, Isaac Sim needs serious hardware. NVIDIA lists an RTX 4080 with 16 GB of VRAM and 32 GB of RAM as the minimum, and Isaac Sim doesn’t support GPUs without RT cores, such as the A100 and H100. If you get stuck, the project has a Discord server.

Arena 4.0: ROS 2 Humble on Ubuntu 22.04

This path installs natively on Ubuntu 22.04. WSL works too, but only with Gazebo. Following the installation guide, run the installer from a fresh terminal, with no ROS 2 sourced and no Python environment active:

curl https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Arena-Rosnav/arena-rosnav/humble/installers/install.sh > install.sh
bash install.sh

Expect it to need more than 80 GB of disk and over an hour, because it compiles ROS 2 Humble from source inside ~/arena4_ws. At the end, it asks whether you want Gazebo, Isaac Sim, and extra planners. If it stops partway, run it again and it picks up where it left off. Then launch a simulation:

cd ~/arena4_ws && . arena.bash
ros2 launch arena_bringup arena.launch.py sim:=gazebo

Always pass sim:=. The default is dummy, which starts no simulator at all. The usage guide lists the other launch arguments.

Arena 3.0: ROS 1 Noetic on Ubuntu 20.04

Choose this path if you need Unity or Flatland, or if you’re reproducing a paper from 2024 or earlier. The master README’s install link is dead, but the original guide survives in the arena3 tag:

curl https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Arena-Rosnav/arena-rosnav/master/install.sh > install.sh
bash install.sh
# then, in a new terminal:
curl https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Arena-Rosnav/arena-rosnav/master/install2.sh > install2.sh
bash install2.sh

The guide asks for about 30 GB of disk and half an hour. Two optional scripts come with it: install3_training.sh adds the training dependencies, and install4_arena_unity.sh downloads the prebuilt Unity simulator (about 480 MB). Then launch:

roslaunch arena_bringup start_arena.launch simulator:=gazebo   # or flatland, unity

The guide pipes these scripts straight into bash. Download them first instead, as above, so their yes/no prompts can read your answers. If the install still fails, a lab that uses Arena 3.0 recommends its ivaROS fork, which installs on Noetic. Keep in mind that ROS Noetic reached end of life on May 31, 2025, so you won’t get ROS updates or security fixes on this path.

When the install breaks

Shuijing Liu, who maintains the awesome-robot-social-navigation list, described Arena 4.0 as “not super easy to install.” The same few problems come up repeatedly in the issue trackers. Here they are, with the fixes that worked:

  1. Packages like cv_bridge, vision_msgs, or pcl_msgs fail to build (4.0). In issue #215, the maintainer’s first suspect is a ROS 2 Humble that’s already sourced in your shell, usually from ~/.bashrc. Comment out source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash, deactivate conda or any venv, open a fresh terminal, and run the installer again.
  2. rosdep is missing on a fresh system. Users in the same thread got further after installing and initializing it: python3-rosdep2 from Ubuntu, or python3-rosdep from the ROS 2 apt repository, then sudo rosdep init and rosdep update.
  3. Downloads fail halfway. One reporter traced part of their errors to a VPN. Fix the network and run the installer again; it resumes.
  4. The docs don’t match your code. Use the docs list above. Issue #219 comes from someone who couldn’t find how to install version 3 at all.
  5. Nothing appears after launch. In 4.0, pass sim:=gazebo or sim:=isaac, since the default is dummy. In 5.0, install the simulator first, or sim:= fails with an install hint.
  6. Docker says “Unknown runtime specified ‘nvidia’” (5.0). Run sudo nvidia-ctk runtime configure --runtime=docker and restart Docker. If RViz crashes with an OpenGL error, add LIBGL_ALWAYS_SOFTWARE=1 to the .env file in your workspace.
  7. Your system changed in ways you didn’t expect. The 4.0 installer offers to delete apt source files for other ROS versions (the default answer is yes), and it adds pyenv and Poetry to your shell config. The ROS 1 installers add lines to ~/.bashrc and ~/.zshrc. Use a spare machine or a fresh Ubuntu install if you can, or the 5.0 container.

Issue #213, opened in July 2025, asks whether Arena 5.0’s Isaac Sim support is open source. It was filed on Arena-Rosnav/arena-rosnav, whose default branch is the ROS 1 master, so the Isaac code isn’t visible there. At the time it was on the humble branch, and today it lives in voshch/Arena. Isaac Sim support matters, because very few social navigation simulators run on the GPU, a gap the same awesome-list thread points out.

See it running

If you’d like to see Arena before installing it, the conference videos show it in action. Here is Arena 3.0 at RSS 2024:
entry.summary: Which Arena-Rosnav (ROS 1, ROS 2 Humble, Jazzy) or SEAN version to install, which simulators each one supports, and fixes for common install errors.
